newsitem.title: BOSNIA: FEATURE - After 50 years, Germans back in Bosnia as peacekeepers.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - After 50 years, Germans back in Bosnia as peacekeepers.

text.p: Germany's occupation of Yugoslavia left irreparable scars on Radmila Cvetkovic.
More than 50 years since Hitler's Wehrmacht retreated from the Balkans in defeat, Cvetkovic, 66, still finds it hard to speak about her experiences in World War Two.

She remembers spending a night of terror listening to Nazi tanks and trucks rolling through her town of Glamoc in western Bosnia in April 1941. "We were so afraid. There were so many tanks and cannons and soldiers. I couldn't sleep."
Neighbours acting in the name of the fascist regime installed by Hitler murdered her family, leaving her an orphan at the age of 11.
"They killed my mother, brother and sister. Hitler set the ideology and the primitives took advantage of it."
Cvetkovic, a Serb, joined the anti-Nazi partisans and spent much of her adolescence fighting the German army and its local fascist allies, the Croatian-led Ustasha.
This month, German combat troops return to the Balkans -- something Cvetkovic never thought she would live to witness.

Breaking a post-war German taboo on deploying ground troops abroad, some 2,000 German soldiers serving under French command are scheduled to join the NATO-led peace force in Bosnia within a couple of weeks.
Cvetkovic is less than enthusiastic about Germany's first full-blown military deployment since World War Two, but she is willing to accept that times have changed.
"It's not so pleasant to hear that they're coming, even after 50 years. But they are not coming as invaders, they are coming as peacekeepers," she said in her modest Sarajevo flat.
"Life has to go on and we have to forgive. Otherwise there would be no end to the hatred."
CIVIL WAR SOWED SEEDS OF LATER CONFLICT
Germany's four-year occupation brought the Holocaust to Yugoslavia and set off a vicious civil war which helped sow the seeds of this decade's conflict in Bosnia and Croatia.
A day after Wehrmacht troops arrived in Sarajevo in 1941, they launched a two-day rampage destroying the contents of the city's mediaeval synagogues.
By the end of 1941, most Jews in Yugoslavia had been executed or sent to their deaths in concentration camps.
A few thousand Jews are left in former Yugoslavia and a mere 500 have stayed in Sarajevo after Bosnia's 1992-95 war.
A prominent member of that tiny Jewish community, Jakob Finci, says he is willing to bury the past.
"I can accept without hesitation German troops as part of NATO's peacekeeping force. Without Germans it's hard to believe NATO can work in Europe."
Finci, 53, said it was time to recognise what many historians have concluded -- that the natives of former Yugoslavia share much of the blame for World War Two atrocities in the Balkans.
"The communist regime decided to blame the Germans for everything that happened here...We have to face the truth -- most of the atrocities were committed by the locals."
Of the estimated one million people that died during the war, historians say the majority were killed by fellow Yugoslavs.
Although Yugoslavia capitulated to the Nazis only days after the invasion, its surrender did not end the fighting.

Communist Partisans led by Josip Broz Tito and Serbian nationalist Chetniks led by Draza Mihailovic took up resistance against the Germans and the puppet Ustasha regime, which slaughtered tens of thousands of Jews, Gypsies and Serbs.
The rival resistance forces, the Partisans and Chetniks, soon fell into a bitter conflict over who would ultimately control Yugoslavia.
What is most painful for Partisan veterans such as Cvetkovic is not the imminent arrival of German troops but having to watch the disintegration of the ideals she fought for as a teenager.
"Bosnia was always about different people living together. I can't believe what happened here."
In 1997, the country that once exploited religious and national differences to conquer the Balkans will be sending soldiers to try to rebuild Bosnia's shattered tradition of co- existence.
This time, Cvetkovic is hoping desperately that German soldiers succeed.
